quotes.citation: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་ཉི་ཤུ་ལྔ་པ། (Kangyur, ཉི་ཁྲི་ vol. ཀ) — the five-eyes section, the question on the divine eye.
quotes.why: The sūtra passage the paragraph quotes, in the Kangyur's own recension of the Twenty-Five Thousand; note ཤཱ་རདྭ་ཏིའི་བུ where the yig cha has ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ. Found by direct search of the canon.

quotes.citation: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་ཉི་ཤུ་ལྔ་པ། (Kangyur) — the continuation of the same answer, after the list of god-realms.
quotes.why: The part of the sūtra passage the paragraph's ཞེས་སོགས་ leaves out, and the one Haribhadra's gloss actually summarises: the bodhisattva's divine eye knows the deaths and births of beings in worlds as many as the Ganges' sands. Found by reading on from the passage above.

quotes.citation: ལེའུ་བརྒྱད་མ། པོད་དང་པོ། — the same sūtra passage in Haribhadra's eight-chapter arrangement of the Twenty-Five Thousand.
quotes.why: The recension whose wording (ཤཱ་རིའི་བུས་གསོལ་པ, ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ) the paragraph's quotation follows; the yig cha abbreviates བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ to བྱང་ཆེན and reads རིགས for རིས.

quotes.citation: མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན། སྐབས་དང་པོ། — the verse listing the ten instructions (གདམས་ངག).
quotes.why: The root-verse line the whole five-eyes section hangs from; the text named it at p405 (སྤྱན་ལྔ་དང་ནི། ཞེས་གསུངས།). Found by direct search.

Haribhadra's gloss, from which the paragraph lifts its second quotation; it pairs each of the five eyes with its object by the order of enumeration (གྲངས་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ), so the second object belongs to the maturation-born divine eye.

A few lines later Haribhadra names a second divine eye, the one born of deliberate cultivation, among the six clairvoyances: the qualifier on the five-eyes divine eye is there to keep the two apart. Found by reading on from the lemma.

Ārya Vimuktisena, the earliest Indian commentator on the Ornament, giving the reason the gods cannot know the bodhisattva's divine eye: its object is the deaths and births of all beings of the ten directions — the object Haribhadra then fixes as the divine eye's.

quotes.citation: ཡུམ་གསུམ་གནོད་འཇོམས། — the gloss dividing the five eyes.
quotes.why: The Bṛhaṭṭīkā (attributed to Vasubandhu) characterises the divine eye by a different object — knowledge of all concentrations and absorptions — a reading Tsongkhapa quotes beside Vimuktisena's. Found by direct search after Jamyang Zhepa cited it.

Tsongkhapa's gloss, which spells out Haribhadra's compressed pair: death is passing from here to elsewhere, birth arriving here from elsewhere, and the eye is born of the maturation of virtuous karma alone.

quotes.citation: ལེགས་བཤད་གསེར་ཕྲེང་། སྐབས་དང་པོ། སྤྱན་ལྔ། — the explanation of the sūtra's god-realms clause, following the Bṛhaṭṭīkā.
quotes.why: Tsongkhapa's reading of the very clause the paragraph quotes — what it means for the bodhisattva to 'know the divine eye' of the Four Great Kings' gods. Found by reading on in the gser phreng.
Gyaltsab Je's gloss on the same words of Haribhadra: the divine eye born of the maturation of prior contaminated virtue knows the deaths and births of all beings as they are. Found by direct search.
Gyaltsab Je's boundary statement — the divine eye from the path of preparation — which Chökyi Gyaltsen quotes at p412 and has to read as a statement of the principal case rather than a pervasion.

Chökyi Gyaltsen, in this same text a few paragraphs on, denying that whatever is a divine eye directly realises the deaths and births of all beings — the very words he quotes from Haribhadra here are not a definition. Found by direct search.

Chökyi Gyaltsen's own definition of the divine eye in his mtha' dpyod: 'all' (ཐམས་ཅད) has been dropped from the object, which is how the definition survives his own objection about gradations of power.

Chökyi Gyaltsen against those who deny a divine eye to a bodhisattva on the path of accumulation: one who has the fourth dhyāna as support has it — which is why Gyaltsab's boundary cannot be a strict one.

Panchen Sonam Drakpa (Loseling) holding that Gyaltsab Je's description of the divine eye as a clear physical faculty, with a sense-consciousness clairvoyance based on it, must be read as provisional — the same fault line Chökyi Gyaltsen works along. Found by reading on from the pack's lead.

Jamyang Zhepa (Gomang) answering the same opponent: the sūtra, describing the bodhisattva's divine eye, only marks its lower and upper limits, so it does not make 'knows the deaths and births of all beings' a pervasion.
